frameworks.name: Ghost Product Trust Architecture
frameworks.definition: A sales framework that recommends alternative products at lower margins (or free alternatives) to establish buyer trust, then upsells higher-margin products based on that trust foundation.

frameworks.name: Prescriptive Close with Habit Stacking
frameworks.definition: A closing method that prescribes exact usage instructions before the ask, pairs products with existing daily habits (toothbrushing, morning routine) to reduce new habit friction, and closes via a simplified one-click decision.

frameworks.name: Consultative Objection Reframe
frameworks.definition: When a buyer claims budget constraints, reframe the removed product in terms of the new behavior it enabled (e.g., 'you'll eat broccoli instead'), shifting the frame from price negotiation to outcome preservation.

claims.text: Recommending cheaper alternatives (ghost products) that a buyer can source elsewhere, when done with genuine intent to serve the buyer's interest, produces 100% close rates on subsequently recommended products. Alex Hormozi implemented this in gym supplement sales, selling to 100% of incoming customers and teaching it to novice salespeople who achieved 80-90% close rates on product recommendations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Retail environment with product bundles
Buyer presents with a pre-made list of recommendations
Seller has genuine belief in remaining products
Intent is aligned with buyer's self-interest, not seller profit
claims.mechanism: When a salesperson recommends alternatives outside their product line, the buyer perceives the seller as prioritizing the buyer's interest over the seller's commission; this trust transfer accelerates acceptance of the seller's core recommendations.

numbers.axis: Close rate on core product recommendations after ghost product recommendation

anchors.value: 100% close rate (Hormozi personally); 80-90% (novice salespeople trained by Hormozi)

bounded_by: Requires seller to genuinely believe the ghost product alternative is legitimate
Tactic fails if intent is manipulative (to create false trust while serving seller's profit)
Does not apply to self-serve, transaction-based sales where trust is not a variable

claims.text: The ethical boundary between manipulation and persuasion is intent. If you change someone's behavior with positive intent to serve them and you believe in what you're selling, you are persuading; if you change behavior with negative intent to exploit, you are manipulating.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Persuasion or sales context where behavior is the outcome
claims.mechanism: Intent determines the direction of the behavior change. The same tactic (recommending alternatives, withholding information) produces different moral effects depending on whether the seller's underlying intention is to maximize the buyer's outcome or to exploit vulnerability.
bounded_by: Assumes buyer cannot independently verify intent; relies on seller's internal state

claims.text: When a customer states they are on a budget, reframe by asking the salesperson to order recommendations by importance (must-have vs. nice-to-have), then remove the lowest-priority item. If the buyer still objects, reframe the removal as a new behavior substitution (e.g., 'you'll need to eat more broccoli') to signal that the removed item is not unimportant, just offset by new effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Buyer expresses budget constraint mid-close
Seller has already established trust
Product is genuinely beneficial, not luxury
claims.mechanism: Reframing cost removal as behavioral substitution (additional effort from buyer) preserves the perceived value of the product and signals seller expertise; it prevents the buyer from concluding that the removed product is worthless.
bounded_by: Assumes the removed item has a legitimate substitute behavior
Fails if the product has no behavioral alternative (pure luxury)

claims.text: Before making a product recommendation close, prescribe exact usage instructions (e.g., 'two in the morning, three with lunch') and ask the buyer to identify an existing daily habit (brushing teeth, drinking coffee) to anchor the new behavior. Pair the new product with that existing habit using visual cues (tape on the toothbrush) to prevent the new behavior from becoming a separate habit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product requires repeated daily consumption or use
Buyer has identified an existing daily routine
claims.mechanism: Habit stacking (pairing a new behavior with an existing cue) reduces the cognitive load of forming a new habit. When the buyer visualizes the implementation (physical placement, trigger), they commit to the behavior before the price ask, increasing close rates.
bounded_by: Only applies to consumption-based or repeat-use products
Does not apply to one-time purchases or high-friction behavior changes

claims.text: After the buyer commits to the close (based on prescriptive instructions and habit stacking), ask 'Do you want to use the card you have on file?' to close via a one-click decision, eliminating wallet removal, payment method selection, and purchase-decision friction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Buyer has pre-authorized a payment method
Prior steps (prescription, habit-stacking, trust-building) have been completed
claims.mechanism: Minimizing the number of decision points before purchase removes friction and leverages the buyer's prior commitment (the prescribed close, the habit stack agreement) to secure payment.
bounded_by: Requires buyer to have previously stored a payment method

claims.text: Low-ticket, high-transaction-volume environments (car washes, nails, hair, massage) are the best training grounds for sales skill development. Completing many low-ticket transactions teaches objection handling, closing mechanics, and customer psychology faster than any course, and this skill transfers to high-ticket sales.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Seller is a novice to intermediate salesperson
Business environment has high transaction volume
claims.mechanism: High-volume, low-stakes transactions provide rapid feedback loops and desensitize the seller to rejection; the multiplication of reps accelerates learning velocity compared to courses or high-ticket sales where feedback is sparse.
bounded_by: Assumes the high-volume business has a scalable sales process to learn from
Benefit diminishes once sales skill is already strong

claims.text: When selling services (e.g., web design) with a long list of optional add-ons, recommend third-party alternatives for out-of-core-competency services (e.g., 'guys in the Philippines can do this cheaper') and position the salesperson as an advocate helping the buyer find the best solution, not just the most profitable one for the company.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with clear core competencies and non-core add-ons
Salesperson (not owner) is executing the tactic
claims.mechanism: Positioning the salesperson as leaning toward the buyer's side of the table (recommending third-party alternatives) builds trust and psychological alignment; the buyer perceives the salesperson as protecting their interest, not maximizing the company's revenue.
bounded_by: Tactic is more effective when salesperson executes it than when owner does (owner recommendation creates suspicion of hidden economics)
Requires that third-party alternative actually exists and is known to the salesperson

claims.text: The goal of a sales conversation is to move from an adversarial table-across position (buyer vs. seller) to a collaborative shoulder-to-shoulder position (both evaluating the same decision). The ghost product recommendation, third-party referral, and consultative reframe all serve this psychological alignment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sales conversation with time for relationship building
claims.mechanism: When the buyer perceives the seller as evaluating the decision from the buyer's side of the table (not across from it), the buyer's defensive skepticism decreases and receptiveness to the seller's recommendations increases.
bounded_by: Does not apply to transactional, one-time, or high-volume low-touch sales

claims.text: If a salesperson is uncomfortable not physically carrying a ghost product (a product recommended but not sold), they may stock it without ever selling it; the psychological benefit of not selling it overrides the carrying cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Seller has inventory capacity
Ghost product has low carrying cost
claims.mechanism: Carrying an unsold product provides psychological permission for the seller to recommend it without guilt; the absence of sales does not harm the tactic's effectiveness.
bounded_by: Only practical for low-cost inventory items
Not applicable to high-carrying-cost or perishable products

claims.text: The ghost products (items recommended to be purchased elsewhere) should be the lowest-margin products in the portfolio. By ceding low-margin sales to competitors, the seller retains trust, and the buyer then purchases the high-margin items, yielding net higher profit than attempting to sell both.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Seller has clear margin hierarchy across product line
Buyer perceives alternatives as viable (product available elsewhere)
claims.mechanism: Margin sacrifice on low-value items funds trust capital, which then drives higher conversion on high-margin items. The net profit is higher because the conversion multiplier from trust exceeds the margin ratio between items.
bounded_by: Does not work if high-margin and low-margin items cannot be separated in the buyer's mind
Requires the low-margin product to have a genuine external alternative

claims.text: A salesperson should project a vision of the buyer's life after purchasing the product (the benefit state) before explaining how to use the product, and certainly before asking for the sale. This vision-first framing makes the prescriptive close more believable and the habit-stack more natural.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product has a clear outcome or benefit state
Buyer has time for consultative conversation
claims.mechanism: Establishing the outcome vision first (benefit, feeling, result) creates the why, which makes the how (prescription, habit-stacking) feel less like an instruction and more like expert guidance toward a desired state.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodity/undifferentiated products where the benefit is unclear

examples.text: At a gym supplement company, a new challenge launched and 100 customers arrived for nutrition orientation. Alex Hormozi had stocked out of a key product. When customers arrived, Hormozi told them: 'You can get this one for cheaper down the street at Costco. This one's a little better, but I think it'll get the job done. You can get this one after you've done the program.' The customer replied 'Oh, thanks. That was cool.' Hormozi then said, 'But you do want this and this from us,' and the customer agreed immediately. Hormozi then tested giving away two cheaper product recommendations, and every customer purchased the higher-margin items. When Hormozi pointed out to a woman that her recommended mass-gainer was inappropriate for her goal and said 'You're not trying to gain mass, are you? You can just cross that out,' the customer trusted the recommendation so deeply that Hormozi closed with the remaining items and a prescriptive habit-stack instruction: 'I need you to take two of these in the morning, put this in your car so you always have it with you.' Every customer at this point purchased.

When closing a supplement sale after recommending three products, Hormozi asked the customer, 'What do you do every morning no matter what? Do you wake up and smoke a cigarette? Do you drink a cup of coffee? Do you take a shower, brush your teeth?' The customer said 'I brush my teeth every morning.' Hormozi then said, 'I don't want you to put this in your cupboard because you'll forget about it. I want you to put it next to your toothbrush. Get a piece of tape, put a 2 on it — I want you to take two of them.' Then Hormozi repeated this process for each product, anchoring the usage to existing daily habits. At the end, Hormozi asked, 'Do you just want to use the card you have on file now?' — a one-click purchase decision. This sequence (habit-stacking + simplified payment ask) closed effectively with customers who had previously been resistant to upsells.

A young salesperson, hired by Hormozi with no prior sales experience, was trained on the ghost product framework. After receiving training on recommending cheaper alternatives and habit-stacking, the salesperson achieved 80-90% close rates on supplement recommendations, compared to Hormozi's own 100% rate. The salesperson's success demonstrated that the tactic was teachable and not dependent on Hormozi's personal charisma or experience level.

Hormozi worked at a business selling low-ticket items (supplements at a gym) with high transaction volume. Over time, Hormozi developed and tested sales mechanics through rapid iteration and feedback: the ghost product tactic emerged by accident when inventory ran out, but subsequent repeated testing with two ghost products confirmed the pattern. Hormozi then generalized the tactic across different product lists and customer types. This high-volume, low-ticket environment was the training ground that enabled the discovery and refinement of the ghost product framework.

When selling web design services with a long list of add-ons, a salesperson can say to a prospect: 'This service isn't our core capability. If we did it, it would cost you more because we'd have to allocate more resources. There are guys in the Philippines who will do it for you. I've got a connection I can talk to you about after this call.' This recommendation positions the salesperson as an advocate, not a mercenary. The prospect then perceives the salesperson as leaning toward the prospect's side of the table. Unbeknownst to the prospect, the salesperson is still selling the core web design services, but the trust from the third-party referral makes the prospect receptive to the core offer.

practices.text: If you work at a low-ticket, high-volume business (car wash, nails, hair, massage), try to inject yourself into the sales process and conduct as many transactions as possible. The repetition will train your sales skills faster than any paid course.

Carry ghost products (items you recommend to be purchased elsewhere) even if you never sell them, if you feel uncomfortable not having them in stock. The psychological permission to recommend them is more valuable than the carrying cost.

When a customer gives a budget objection, reframe by asking them to identify which recommended items are 'must-have' vs. 'nice-to-have,' remove the lowest-priority item, and explain the new behavior substitution (e.g., eating more broccoli) so the customer doesn't perceive the removed item as worthless.

Before closing a sale on a consumption-based product, ask the customer what daily habit they already have (brushing teeth, drinking coffee, showering) and anchor the new product usage to that existing habit with a physical cue (tape with a number, placement next to toothbrush) to prevent the new behavior from becoming a separate habit.

When presenting product recommendations, paint a vision of the customer's life after using the product before explaining how to use it. This vision-first order makes the prescriptive instructions feel like expert guidance toward a desired state, not an arbitrary instruction.
